questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Quoting a field that holds the delimiter
questions.learningObjective: explain why a field containing the delimiter must be wrapped
questions.stem: A record is written as three comma-separated fields, and the middle field holds the text "Doe, Jane". A reader that cuts at every comma sees four pieces, not three. What rule makes those three fields legible?

options.text: A field holding the delimiter is wrapped in quotes, so the comma inside belongs to the value
The delimiter is renegotiated per record, so a record with commas in it picks another one
options.misconception: believes the delimiter is renegotiated per record rather than quoted

options.text: The field is written once per comma, so each piece reads back as a field of its own
options.misconception: believes a repeated value stands in for quoting

options.text: The value is shortened to Doe, so the comma disappears and the field count returns to three
options.misconception: believes data is truncated to fit a field count

questions.explanation: Quoting is what tells the reader that a delimiter inside quotes is part of a value rather than the end of a field, and the run confirmed it: a scanner that honours the quotes returned the three fields 7, Doe, Jane and 42, while a routine that cut at every comma handed back four pieces with a stray quote character glued to two of them. Renegotiating the delimiter per record would make the file unreadable by any other program, writing the field once per comma would multiply the data, and shortening the value destroys the data the record exists to carry.
questions.hint: Ask what marks the comma as part of a value rather than the end of a field.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Escaping a quote inside a quoted field
questions.learningObjective: say how a reader tells a closing quote from a literal one
questions.stem: A quoted field must itself carry a double quote, so the value is He said "go". Quoting it alone would close the field at the first inner quote. How does a reader tell the two apart?

options.text: The inner quote is doubled, so a pair inside quotes is one literal quote and a lone one closes
A backslash escapes it, which is the same trick a programming language uses
options.misconception: believes record files reuse programming-language escape rules

options.text: The field is left unquoted and the quote stays in the value exactly as written
options.misconception: believes an inner quote needs no escaping outside quotes

options.text: The quote is dropped, since a quote character carries nothing worth storing
options.misconception: believes quote characters are discarded rather than encoded

questions.explanation: Once quotes are the escape mechanism, a quote inside a quoted field has to be distinguishable from the quote that ends the field, and doubling it is the choice that needs no extra character and no new rule: the reader reads a doubled pair as one literal quote and a single quote as the end. A backslash would drag the rules of a programming language into a data file and would itself need escaping whenever a real backslash appeared. Dropping the character loses information, and leaving the field unquoted only works until the value happens to contain the delimiter.
questions.hint: Ask how the reader tells the quote that closes the field from one inside it.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Scanning a record that holds a quoted comma
questions.learningObjective: trace a quote-aware scanner over one record
questions.stem:
text := '7,"Doe, Jane",42'
fields := []   i := 0
WHILE i < LENGTH(text):
    IF text[i] = '"':
        j := i + 1
        WHILE text[j] <> '"':  j := j + 1
        fields.APPEND(SUBSTRING(text, i + 1, j - i - 1))
        i := j + 1
    ELSE:
        j := i
        WHILE text[j] <> ',':  j := j + 1
        fields.APPEND(SUBSTRING(text, i, j - i))
        i := j
    IF text[i] = ',':  i := i + 1
DISPLAY LENGTH(fields)

options.text: 3, because the scanner only treats a comma as a separator outside the quotes
4, because one field is counted for every comma the record holds anywhere
options.misconception: believes the scanner splits on commas inside a quoted field

options.text: 2, because the quoted run also swallows the plain field that follows it
options.misconception: believes the closing quote ends the scan instead of the field

options.text: 5, because the opening quote character starts a field of its own
options.misconception: believes the quote character is counted as a field in its own right

questions.explanation: The scanner takes the quoted branch at the second character, so the comma inside the quotes never reaches the separator test, and it appends one field for the run between the quotes rather than one per comma. Running it returned 3, and the fields were 7, Doe, Jane and 42, which is what the writer meant. The answer of 4 is the count a plain cut-at-every-comma routine produces, and it is tempting because that routine is far shorter; the other two counts come from placing the closing quote wrongly.
questions.hint: Follow the branch taken at the second character, where a quote opens the field.

questions.topic: A value that holds a line break
questions.learningObjective: predict what a line-based reader does with a quoted line break
questions.stem: A free-text note holds two lines separated by a line break, the field is quoted, and the rest of the file is one record per line. What does a reader that treats every line as a record do?

options.text: It cuts the record in two, so the note’s second line is read as the start of a new record
It joins the two lines, because an open quote tells it to fold the break into the field
options.misconception: believes quoting alone makes a line-based reader repair the split

options.text: It stops at the break and reports the note as truncated, refusing to read further
options.misconception: believes a line-based reader detects the break and stops cleanly

options.text: It reads the note as one field, since the quotes are still open across the two lines
options.misconception: believes an open quote is enough to make a line-based reader continue

questions.explanation: A reader that finds records by looking for line breaks has already made its decision before it looks at any quote, so the break inside the field ends the record exactly as if the field had ended there, and the second line arrives as a fresh record with the note's tail in its first field. Quoting tells a scanner that tracks quotes, not one that tracks lines. Repairing the split means a reader built to track quotes, and simply stopping turns a formatting problem into a data loss.
questions.hint: Ask whether the reader finds its records by line breaks or by quotes.

R3 alone, because only a missing field breaks a reader while an extra one is harmless
options.misconception: believes an unexpected extra field causes no misalignment

options.misconception: believes a short record is safe to read as it stands

questions.learningObjective: say what a field-count check buys and where it must run
questions.stem: One row of a four-field file arrives holding three fields, so the values after it land in the wrong columns. A reader checks the field count on every row as it reads. What does that check buy, and what does it not do?

options.text: It names the offending row on the spot and stops that row from reaching the columns
It supplies the missing value, so the row is stored with a stand-in in its place
options.misconception: believes a field-count check supplies the value that is absent

options.text: It re-reads the file under a different delimiter, so the short row parses correctly
options.misconception: believes a wrong field count is cured by changing the delimiter

options.text: It certifies every later row, since one conforming row proves the layout holds
options.misconception: believes checking one row certifies the rows that follow it

questions.explanation: A field-count check is a comparison against the number the layout promises, and it is worth exactly as much as the point at which it runs: on every row, as it is read, it names the row that disagrees and stops that row's values before they are written into columns that do not belong to them. The check supplies nothing, since a missing value is not derivable from the count, and changing the delimiter would only invent a different set of problems. Checking one row proves nothing about the rest, which is why a whole file scanned once would leave the same fault invisible.

questions.topic: Locating a field by offset
questions.learningObjective: state what a fixed-width layout depends on
questions.stem: A fixed-width record gives every field a start position and a length, so the quantity is always read from byte 10 for three bytes. What does this layout depend on to keep working?

options.text: Every record keeping the same offsets, because a field is found by position not by content
Every value being written right-aligned, so padding never moves a field’s start
options.misconception: believes the alignment of the text is what fixes the offsets

options.text: Every record being the same length, so the reader can skip on without a separator
options.misconception: confuses a fixed record length with fixed field offsets

options.text: Every field being quoted, so a delimiter inside a value cannot move the fields after it
options.misconception: believes quoting is what makes a fixed-width layout safe

Right-aligning the text is about how a value looks printed and changes nothing about where the next field starts, and a fixed record length is a separate property that lets the reader step to the next record without reading a separator. questions.topic: Reading fixed-width fields from a shifted record
questions.learningObjective: trace a positional read across an over-long value

a := '0042RIVERA00712.50'
b := '0042RIVERAJ00712.50'
READ(s, start, len) := SUBSTRING(s, start, len)
DISPLAY READ(a, 10, 3)
DISPLAY READ(b, 10, 3)

007 then 007, because a positional read always lands on the quantity field
options.misconception: believes fixed offsets ignore a value that is too long

options.text: J00 then 007, because the reader realigns on the last separator it found
options.misconception: believes a fixed-width reader searches for separators

options.text: 00R then 00R, because the offsets are counted back from the end of the record
options.misconception: believes fixed-width offsets are measured from the record’s end

questions.learningObjective: read a byte dump and diagnose the misaligned row
questions.stem: A file gives id four bytes, name six, quantity three and price five, so a sound record is eighteen bytes. The dump shows row 1 read as 0042, RIVERA, 007 and 12.50, and row 2 read as 0043, RIVERA, J00 and 709.7. What has happened to row 2?

options.text: Its name ran one byte long, so the quantity field reads across the boundary as J00
Its quantity is genuinely J00, because the file stores a quantity beginning with a letter
options.misconception: believes a letter in a numeric field is a real stored value

options.text: Its offsets are all correct, because a byte dump always shows the true field boundaries
options.misconception: believes a positional dump cannot misstate a boundary

options.text: The row is one byte short, so the reader ran off its end and padded the rest
options.misconception: believes a short record is the cause of a shifted field

A stored value of J00 is not a possibility, because the quantity field is numeric, and a short row would leave blanks rather than digits from the next field. The diagnostic rule is that a run of fields that is right up to one point and wrong from there on marks a value that overran its slot.
questions.hint: Find the first field that stops matching, then check whether one byte explains everything after it.

questions.subject: COMPUTING_FOUNDATIONS
questions.topic: Bytes occupied by fixed-width records with a separator
questions.learningObjective: compute the size of a fixed-width file
questions.stem: A fixed-width record gives id four bytes, name ten, quantity three and price six, and the writer appends a one-byte record separator after every record including the last. A file holds one hundred such records. How many bytes does the file occupy?
questions.explanation: The four fields take 4 + 10 + 3 + 6, which is 23 bytes, and the trailing separator makes each record 24, so one hundred records take 100 times 24, which is 2400 bytes. Multiplying the field bytes by the record count and adding the separators separately reaches the same figure: 100 times 23 is 2300, plus 100 separators is 2400. The separator after the final record is the detail that is easy to leave out, and leaving it out gives 2300, a file that is one byte short of the width the reader will step by.
questions.hint: Work out the bytes in one record including its separator, then multiply by the record count.

Two readers disagreeing over which half of a multi-byte character comes first
options.misconception: believes a leading marker byte sets byte order

options.text: A file being opened by a program expecting a different character encoding
options.misconception: believes the marker byte declares the encoding

questions.topic: A naming line at the front of a file
questions.learningObjective: explain why a leading naming line defeats a positional read
questions.stem: The first line of a file names its columns and the lines after it hold the values. A reader seeks to byte zero and then takes a fixed number of bytes per record. What goes wrong, and why?

A reported change stops the read, so the cost is a failed run and an alert, and the data on disk is untouched and correct. An unseen change produces a clean-looking result built from values the reader did not expect, and the file itself is still perfectly valid, so the next reader, the report written from it and the decision made on that report all inherit the mistake without a single point at which someone could have noticed. A positional reader that stops at its expected field count is the worst case, because appending leaves every offset before it unchanged: the reader is not even reading the wrong bytes, it is reading the right ones and declining to go further. The general shape is that a change the format cannot represent as a change is a change nobody can audit.

questions.explanation: A reported change costs a failed run and an alert, and the file on disk is untouched, so the cost is bounded and the moment of detection is known. The change described here costs nothing anywhere, because the reader is not reading the wrong bytes, it is reading the right ones and declining to go further, and the file itself is perfectly valid. A self-describing header would have named the extra field and let the reader report it, which is why the format is part of the answer and not just the reader. Once a wrong value has entered a store there is no later point at which the error is visible, since every copy inherits it unremarked.

answer.exemplar: The second walk assigns a node its distance the first time it reaches it, and it reaches nodes in order of distance, so when a node is first given a distance of d there has already been an attempt at every smaller distance and none of them reached it. The first route of that length is therefore the shortest one, and no later arrival can improve it. The depth-first walk has no such order: it may reach a node by a long route while a much shorter route to the same node was sitting unexplored on a branch it had backed out of, and it only discovers the better route afterwards, having already recorded the worse one. Nothing about the graph stops that, because a node can be reached by any number of routes of any lengths. The condition that makes the second walk safe is that every link counts the same, since a link is counted as one step whether it is cheap or expensive; as soon as the links carry different costs the first route found is no longer necessarily the cheapest, and the argument no longer holds.

questions.explanation: The guarantee comes from the order of arrival rather than from the walking itself. A walk that works outward reaches every node at distance 1 before any at distance 2, so the first time a node is reached the route taken is as short as any route could be, and a later route can only match it or be worse. A walk that goes deep first has no such order: it can reach a node by a long route while a shorter one sits unexplored on a branch it backed out of, and by the time it finds the better route it has already recorded the worse one. Running both over the same graph gave 3 for the outward walk on every node and produced a route of 4 for one node, which is what the two orders cost.
